posts.content_md:
This is my most recent H1H2 (hologram number 24.1... (-: ). They have been coming out MUCH better since I got a clue about polarization and interference patterns... The star shaped thing (its a Christmas ornament) is about 2 inches in front of the film, the lion on the left can only be seen if you look around the edge of the plate. 'tis a lousy image, but the outtakes were even worse... The image is actualy much greener than this makes it look. 

VRP-M plate, JD-2 chemistry, beam ratio of 2:1 (ref:obj), 120 microjoules/cm^2 (10 seconds). (maybe... my meter hasn't been calibrated since the 80's, and it was for 632 nm, not 532 nm), 315M laser. The H1 was on VRP-M film.

What is the best-practices beam ratio with VRP-M? 

There is a grating right on the plane of the plate which distracts from the image... Is that from the infamous wood-grain (and addressed with Brewser's angle), or is it from not having a spatial filter?

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
If you put a white card in the plate holder and look at the reference beam, it should be perfectly even. If there are rings then you need to clean the optics or use a spatial filter.

Thank for the picture. I don't yet use VRP but I think the ratio should be closer to 1 to 1.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:c9258965c9]What is the best-practices beam ratio with VRP-M? [/quote:c9258965c9] 

1:1. This is the best ratio for any reflection, however, it's more important for VRP because VRP is more sensitive to variations in ratio. 

[quote:c9258965c9]There is a grating right on the plane of the plate which distracts from the image... Is that from the infamous wood-grain (and addressed with Brewser's angle), or is it from not having a spatial filter?[/quote:c9258965c9]

No, it's probably from bad baffling (carding). A stray refelction (actually two stray reflections) from something shiny on the table, or perhaps from the plate holder, probably ended up interfering on the plate creating a grating.

posts.author: Tommy
posts.content_md:
I've painted everything black... And added lots of baffles... And a beam ratio of 1:1... I definitely need a spatial filter, but that'll take a bit more work. 

So I was pondering the hologram some more, and realized that the green which I thought was on the plane of the film was actualy an image of the H1. It looked like it was on the film because it was "larger" than the film and there were no depth cues. Light was scattering off the film, and showing up extremely well. Flip it over and look at the other image, and theres a bright green rectangle off in the distance...

So, next question... How can I reduce the light scattering off the H1? I've been bleaching my transmission holograms the same way as my reflection holograms (JD-2 chemistry). Is that best practices?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: If light is scattering off the H1 from the H1 reconstruction (H2 object), so that the H1 is actually holographically imaging on the H2 then either something is pretty dirty or or the H1 is too noisy and too cloase. Try washing the H1 and gently rubing the film under the water with either fingers or a soft cloth. Be careful that you rub gently or you'll scratch the emulsion. If you have the coherence, take the H1 back. The H2 image will also be off the image plane and too far back or forward, depending which direction you take the H1, but you can judge whether the H1 image is better by taking the H1 back. Bleaching in JD2 (I'm assuming that's a Pot Dichromate bleach) may be noisy, which cause this effect. You could try not bleaching or not completely bleaching (leave it a little grey). The H2 will be dim, but again, you can see how much the H1 images. Another possibility is that a stray beam hit the H1 and caused scatter to the H2. So painting everything black and baffling well may help. However, remember that black objects also scatter

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: One last thing to think about the the beam ratio when making the H1. If it is too high the master will be noisy.
